summary:
We built SPHEREx Data Player so anyone can explore NASA’s wideband infrared sky images. Sky View gives people new to astronomy a sky map so they can search by object name or directly click on map to choose the desired field. Users who know already details can work directly with right ascension and declination (RA and Dec), dates filter along with field size then compare exposures, Spectral brightness, flux, and export measurements.

The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is one of six prefetched examples which is also part of our final demo. In the demo, we find the comet in Sky View and compare two August 8, 2025 exposures using the same display settings. The cloud around the comet appears brighter at 4.230 µm than at 4.158 µm. A pixel spectrum from the August observations peaks near 4.26 µm, consistent with the carbon dioxide emission reported by the SPHEREx team.
details:
We built SPHEREx Data Player around a simple question: how can someone go from spotting an object on a sky map to examining the measurements behind it and answer some research question about it? Sky View gives first-time users a place to start. They can search the vast catalog of already identified objects by name and resize a box around the part of the sky they want to explore. Users who want to go deeper can enter right ascension and declination (RA and Dec), filter by dates, and open the original exposures.

The player comes with six prefetched examples: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, and 3I/ATLAS. We chose 3I/ATLAS for the demo because it shows how images and spectra answer different questions about the same object and available in case internet connection turns bad. We find the comet in Sky View, open its August 2025 observations, and compare two August 8 exposures on the same brightness scale. The coma appears brighter at 4.230 µm than at 4.158 µm. The August pixel spectrum peaks near 4.26 µm, consistent with the carbon dioxide emission reported by the SPHEREx team.

Most of our creativity went into bringing the map, images, and measurements together in an accurate and insightful manner. A user can click a pixel(s) or draw around a region and immediately see a spectrum for each selected pixel. They can pin a reading, check its uncertainty and source exposure, and export it as CSV. We also considered how to show a moving target clearly. Fixed Sky Blink holds the background sky in place so the comet’s predicted position moves across the frame. Comet-centered playback keeps the comet in view across observations taken farther apart.

We used JavaScript and Canvas for the interface, and Python with Astropy and NumPy to read calibrated FITS files from the SPHEREx database, calculate wave planes, and align the images. The server checks memory and then a SQLite disk cache before contacting NASA/IPAC. It saves downloaded cutouts and completed searches for reuse. Live searches use SPHEREx DR1 and QR3. The local build includes the prefetched examples and sky catalog for offline use. The public version runs on Google Cloud Run with temporary cache storage on each instance.

Our goal is to make NASA’s infrared observations approachable in a classroom and research setting and useful for follow-up exploration. We designed for people with different levels of astronomy experience and different internet connections. We kept the original exposure links so someone who notices an interesting feature can trace it back to the observation.
